\title{\Large PlanArena: validated decision support and optimization for land-use change\\[0.3em]
\large Parcel-level impacts, likelihood and recommendations on official data for ten US cities}
\author{Parya Payami\\ \small Department of Architecture, University of Wisconsin--Milwaukee}
\date{Draft, \today}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
\noindent Planners decide land-use changes parcel by parcel. Planning support tools rarely show together what a
change would do, whether zoning and the adopted plan allow it, how likely it is and which alternatives would do
better, and they rarely test these outputs against what happened. PlanArena is an open decision support system that
provides all of these for 4{,}995{,}208 parcels in ten large US cities, built from official land-use, plan and
zoning data. Any edit is scored on 11 social, economic and environmental indicators in
45 ms (Manhattan) to 0.57 s (New York City). A redevelopment model estimates how likely the change
is, an optimizer recommends plans, and voting rules compare how stakeholders would decide. Each component was tested
on observed outcomes. In Manhattan, predicted effects of 2015--2025 changes correlated with recorded homes ($r =
0.840$) and emissions ($r = 0.857$), and redevelopment was ranked out of time with an AUC of
0.847--0.952. In seven cities, zoning and plans added little to predicting where development happens
but helped predict what it becomes. Likelihood weighting brought projections of new homes from 76--193
to 0.81--2.64 times what was built. The optimizer found the exact optimum in 93\% of small test
areas.
\end{abstract}

\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} planning support systems; decision support; land-use optimization; urban digital twins;
impact assessment; model validation

\section{Introduction}

Land-use change in US cities is decided parcel by parcel. Rezonings, amendments to comprehensive plans and approvals
of conversions are justified by their expected effects on housing, jobs, services, the tax base and the environment.
To weigh a proposed change, a planner needs to know five things about each affected parcel:
\begin{enumerate}
\item what exists;
\item what zoning permits;
\item what the adopted plan intends;
\item what is likely to happen;
\item what alternative would do better, and what each option would do across these aspects.
\end{enumerate}
Planning support systems and urban digital twins aim to provide this information
\citep{klosterman1999,geertman2020,batty2018,lehtola2022}.

Three gaps limit how far planners can rely on such tools.
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Testing.} Their outputs are seldom tested against what happened. Reviews of planning support systems
and urban digital twins find that claimed capabilities run ahead of demonstrated ones
\citep{vonk2005,lei2023,azadi2025,kruse2026}. Scenario tools commonly project development at capacity, assuming that
each site builds out to what the rules allow. In three Manhattan rezonings replayed in this paper, capacity projected
8{,}423 homes on development sites; 561 had been built by 2025.
\item \textbf{Plausibility.} Land-use optimization generates plans that score well on chosen objectives
\citep{malczewski2006,rahman2021,zheng2023}. It rarely asks whether the recommended changes are plausible, or how the
choice among plans depends on the decision rule used to make it \citep{brandt2016,feng2024,lin2025}.
\item \textbf{Data.} Existing land use, zoning and the adopted plan are published by different agencies in different
schemas. Some plans exist only as documents: Philadelphia's land-use plan exists only as maps in 17 PDF
district plans.
\end{itemize}

This paper presents PlanArena, an open parcel-level decision support system, and tests each of its components on
observed outcomes. The contributions are as follows.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{An integrated system.} For every parcel, PlanArena combines what exists, what is permitted, what is
planned, what is likely and what is recommended. Any edit is scored on 11 indicators across three
pillars (social, economic and environmental), with sensitivity ranges, at interactive speed. A multi-objective
optimizer recommends plans within zoning and precedent, and the system compares how alternative decision rules would
choose among them.
\item \textbf{Official data for ten cities.} The official existing land use, adopted plan and zoning for
4{,}995{,}208 parcels are put on one schema. A validated method turns a plan published only as vector PDF maps
into a parcel layer.
\item \textbf{Validation of every component on observed data} (Table~\ref{tab:design}). This covers existing
conditions, reproduction of environmental reviews, effects of observed change, forward prediction of redevelopment,
a cross-city test of what zoning and plans add, scenario projections, and optimizer quality and plausibility.
\item \textbf{Design guidance from the evidence.} The results show which layers a tool should rely on for which
question, and how it should present projections and decisions.
\end{enumerate}

The scope is stated throughout. Impacts are validated against observed data in Manhattan; elsewhere the coefficients
are national or regional. The stakeholder votes are simulated, not elicited. Usability with planners is not
evaluated here.

\section{Related work}\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Planning support systems and urban digital twins.} Planning support systems combine land suitability,
demand projection and allocation in scenario planning \citep{klosterman1999,geertman2020}, often within a geodesign
workflow that links representation, change, impact and decision \citep{steinitz2012}. Their limited use and uncertain
usefulness are long-standing concerns \citep{vonk2005,tebrommelstroet2013,pelzer2017}. Urban digital twins extend the
idea to integrated, updatable city models \citep{batty2018,batty2024,white2021,lehtola2022,ferrebigorra2022}. Reviews
report technical and organisational barriers \citep{lei2023,wu2025} and a gap between ambitions and demonstrated
contributions to planning \citep{azadi2025,luo2025,kruse2026}. PlanArena responds by attaching a test against observed
data to each output it reports.

\paragraph{Land-use optimization and collective decisions.} GIS multicriteria analysis and multi-objective
optimization generate and rank land-use alternatives \citep{malczewski2006,rahman2021}, recently with deep
reinforcement learning \citep{zheng2023} and with explicit stakeholder interests \citep{feng2024,lin2025}. Planning
problems have no single correct solution \citep{rittel1973}, so the rule that turns stakeholder preferences into a
choice matters. Bargaining \citep{nash1950} and voting rules have different properties
\citep{schulze2011,brandt2016}. Bargaining has been combined with allocation in land reallocation \citep{hashemi2026}.
Simulated votes are not participation \citep{arnstein1969}; PlanArena uses them only to show how sensitive a choice is
to its rule.

\paragraph{Predicting development, and the role of regulations.} Urban change models range from cellular automata
\citep{clarke1997} and statistical site models \citep{landis1998} to behavioural simulation \citep{waddell2002,
waddell2003} and agent-based models \citep{parker2003}, with neighbourhood and temporal effects as priorities
\citep{verburg2004,weerasinghe2025}. At the parcel level, models capture existing and historical neighbourhood
conditions \citep{tepe2020}, and machine learning complements econometric analysis of redevelopment
\citep{carruthers2024}. Redevelopment depends on land value relative to the existing structure \citep{rosenthal1994,
dye2007}; in Chicago, smaller and older buildings with less lot coverage are replaced more often
\citep{weber2006,charles2013}.

Regulation matters too, but it is not exogenous:
\begin{itemize}
\item rezoning follows development opportunity \citep{gabbe2018};
\item causal studies of upzoning differ on its short-run effect on construction \citep{freemark2020,dong2024,
greenaway2023};
\item plans are only partly implemented \citep{talen1996,laurian2004,brody2005,berke2006,loh2011};
\item recent land-change models integrate zoning and planning regulations \citep{hersperger2018,domingo2021,
abolhasani2026}, but do not test what those layers add to prediction on held-out history.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Validation.} Land-change predictions should be compared with persistence at several resolutions
\citep{pontius2008,pontius2011}, with transition probabilities validated directly \citep{black2023}. Under spatial and
temporal dependence, random cross-validation overstates skill \citep{roberts2017,ploton2020}, and models apply only
where new data resemble their training data \citep{meyer2021}. Uncertainty from many coefficients is better
represented by varying them jointly \citep{saltelli2019}.

\section{The system}\label{sec:system}

Figure~\ref{fig:arch} shows the architecture. A parcel twin holds each city's official layers. Four engines then
answer the planner's questions:
\begin{itemize}
\item the impact engine: what would this change do?
\item the likelihood models: is it likely?
\item the optimizer: what would do better?
\item the decision module: who would choose it, under which rule?
\end{itemize}
The Studio, a browser application, lets a planner paint uses and floor-area ratios on parcels and see every
indicator, flag and recommendation update.

\subsection{Parcel twin and official layers}

The twin covers the nine largest US cities other than San Jose, and Milwaukee (Table~\ref{tab:cities}).
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Existing land use} is the parcel land use published by the city or its regional planning agency,
refined with assessor records where the layer groups uses.
\item \textbf{The adopted plan} (future land use) and \textbf{zoning} are separate layers.
\item \textbf{Classes.} Every source code is translated by an explicit crosswalk into 16 classes. These are three
housing types, mixed use, retail, office, hotel, industry, warehousing, education, health, civic, open space,
transportation, parking and vacant land, and they nest in nine analysis groups.
\item \textbf{Buildings.} Floor area, homes, year built and assessed value come from assessor or city records, with
estimated fields flagged. Jobs are fitted to Census LEHD block counts.
\end{itemize}
Every input is downloaded by script, with its URL and SHA-256 hash recorded. Philadelphia publishes its plan only as
PDF maps. Appendix~\ref{app:digitise} describes how the maps are digitised: 15 of 17 plans
were converted, covering 83\% of parcels, with median registration errors of 1.1--7.2
ft, and each was checked against a shifted-map control. Where a city publishes no plan as data, the plan layer is
absent rather than estimated.

\subsection{Impact engine}

An edit sets a parcel's use, and optionally its floor-area ratio (FAR). The engine computes the
11 indicators of Table~\ref{tab:indicators} for the parcels within a ten-minute walk and for the city.
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Unchanged parcels} keep their observed values, so the baseline reproduces the records exactly.
\item \textbf{Changed parcels} follow a hybrid delta rule. If only density changes and the record is consistent, the
parcel's observed composition is scaled. If the use changes, the observed old use is removed and the modelled new use
added. The rule was chosen on observed change (Section~\ref{sec:r-change}).
\item \textbf{Derived quantities.} Homes follow from residential floor area and each parcel's floor area per home.
Jobs follow from floor-area components and rates fitted to LEHD block counts. Emissions follow from energy use
intensities and emission factors derived from New York's energy benchmarking data (Local Law 84) and its emission
limits (Local Law 97). Runoff follows from surface coefficients. Assessed value changes by the difference between
modelled values.
\item \textbf{Access indicators} (parks, services and facilities within a walk, land-use mix, green cover) are
recomputed on a 50 m raster.
\item \textbf{Ranges.} Every coefficient has a source and a status, and low and high variants give a sensitivity
range for each indicator.
\end{itemize}
Indicators are combined into pillar scores with weights the planner can change. Scoring a 50-parcel edit takes
45 ms on Manhattan's 42{,}075 parcels and 0.57 s on New York City's 856{,}634,
including the ranges. Impacts are computed for the nine analysis groups, for which the coefficients are calibrated and
validated.

\subsection{Likelihood, precedent and pattern}

Three models tell the planner whether a change is plausible.
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Redevelopment.} A gradient-boosted model (LightGBM) gives each lot's probability of redevelopment
within one, three or five years, and its likely new use. It is trained only on outcomes known at the decision year.
Its features describe the lot (use, size, built and permitted floor area, age, land share of value), its
neighbourhood and its zoning.
\item \textbf{Precedent.} A conversion is flagged when buildings of that use and size have not been converted to the
proposed use in the past decade.
\item \textbf{Pattern consistency.} A graph neural network over parcel adjacency, combined with LightGBM, describes
how well a use fits its surroundings. It describes existing patterns, not what is desirable.
\end{itemize}
Each edit is also flagged when it departs from the adopted plan or from what zoning allows.

\subsection{Optimizer}

The optimizer recommends plans that raise the weighted pillar score, minus a penalty per conversion, under a budget
of changes.
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Constraints.} Zoning is a hard constraint, and conversions without precedent are skipped. Optionally,
moves are weighted by their likelihood.
\item \textbf{Search.} Two methods are provided:
  \begin{itemize}
  \item iterated best response over first-order estimates of each move, with exact re-scoring of the best moves;
  \item a reference-point evolutionary algorithm (NSGA-III; \citealp{deb2014}) that returns a Pareto set across the
  pillars.
  \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}
Both report the best plan found, not a proven optimum.

\subsection{Decision module}

Planning choices are contested \citep{rittel1973}. The decision module shows how the choice among candidate plans
depends on the decision rule.
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Stakeholder agents.} Five agents (residents, business, developers, environmental and city-finance
interests) score each candidate from assumed utilities over the indicators.
\item \textbf{Rules.} Nine voting rules, including Schulze's method \citep{schulze2011}, which decides, are compared
with the Nash bargaining solution \citep{nash1950} and with a residents' referendum by block.
\item \textbf{Checks.} The module reports whether a Condorcet winner exists, whether one insincere ballot could change
the outcome, and how robust the winner is to the assumed coefficients and seats.
\end{itemize}
The utilities are assumptions the planner can edit. The output is a simulated scenario, not public support
\citep{arnstein1969}.

\subsection{Interface and interoperability}

Planners can work in the Studio in two ways: edit parcels by click, box, lasso or search; or upload plans as tables
or GIS files, which are reviewed before they are applied. Studies are stored with a hash-chained audit log. Exports
include a staff-report draft, CSV and GeoJSON files, and a provenance record of every coefficient. A phone version
presents the same engine as a game. Any city or district can be exported to ArcGIS Urban: its space-use, zoning and
land-use types, boundaries, and parcels with a PlanArena scenario.

\section{Validation design}\label{sec:validation}

Each component is tested against observed data (Table~\ref{tab:design}). Wherever outcomes are predicted, models are
trained on one period and tested on a later one. Uncertainty is estimated by resampling spatial tiles
\citep{kunsch1989}, and random splits are avoided \citep{roberts2017}.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\scriptsize
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}
\caption{Validation design: each component of the system and its test against observed data.}
\label{tab:design}
\begin{tabular}{lp{5.6cm}p{4.2cm}l}
\toprule
Component & Question & Data & Section \\
\midrule
Existing conditions & Does the twin reproduce what is there? & LL84 energy, LODES jobs, recorded homes & \ref{sec:r-existing} \\
Planning calculations & Does it reproduce a review's projection from the review's own inputs? & FEIS site tables (two rezonings) & \ref{sec:r-existing} \\
Effects of change & Given an observed change, does it predict the effect? & MapPLUTO 2015 vs 2025 & \ref{sec:r-change} \\
Likelihood & Does it rank lots that redevelop, forward in time? & Rolling origins 2016--2025 & \ref{sec:r-likely} \\
Official layers & What do zoning and plans add, in other cities? & Seven city panels & \ref{sec:r-layers} \\
Scenario projections & Are projected homes close to what was built? & Four cities; three rezonings & \ref{sec:r-homes} \\
Optimizer & How close is the best plan found to the optimum? & Exhaustive search; 12 districts & \ref{sec:r-opt} \\
Realism & Are recommended changes plausible? & 2020 plans vs 2025 outcomes & \ref{sec:r-opt} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The cross-city test (Section~\ref{sec:r-layers}) uses seven cities with parcel histories (Appendix
Table~\ref{tab:panels}).
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Outcomes.} Development is defined as each source records it: a new building or a large increase in
floor area (Los Angeles, Dallas, New York), a new building (Milwaukee), a change of use class between land-use
inventories (Phoenix, San Diego), or a new-construction permit (Chicago).
\item \textbf{Blocks.} Four feature blocks are added in turn: existing conditions (E), neighbourhood context within
400 m (C), zoning (Z) and the adopted plan (P).
\item \textbf{Leakage controls.} Where a zoning or plan layer is current rather than historical but its changes are
dated, a conservative variant drops lots whose zoning or plan dates from the window's start or later.
\end{itemize}

\section{Results}\label{sec:results}

\subsection{Existing conditions and planning calculations}\label{sec:r-existing}

The twin reproduces Manhattan's existing conditions:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Emissions.} Modelled building emissions match 6{,}234 benchmarked buildings in a year not used for
fitting (log--log $r = 0.807$, median error 31\%, total 1.04 times metered).
\item \textbf{Jobs.} Modelled jobs correlate with LEHD counts at tract level ($r = 0.843$) and less well at
block level ($r = 0.727$).
\item \textbf{Homes.} Given the observed use and floor area of 295 lots developed in 2015--2025, the estimated
homes total is 1.04 times the recorded count ($r = 0.903$).
\item \textbf{Environmental reviews.} Given the reviews' own sites, floor area and uses, PlanArena reproduces the
projected homes of two rezoning reviews at 0.86 and 1.00 times the review figures.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Effects of observed change}\label{sec:r-change}

The engine predicts the effects of real changes better than a simple baseline (Table~\ref{tab:change}). For
3{,}350 lots that changed in Manhattan between 2015 and 2025, each was given its 2015 state and its observed new
use and floor area.
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Correlation.} The predicted change in homes correlates with the recorded change at $r = 0.840$,
against $r = 0.427$ for the mean change of the same transition type. Assessed value is at $r =
0.870$ against 0.148, and emissions of the 194 benchmarked changed buildings at $r =
0.857$ against 0.090.
\item \textbf{Totals.} The engine overestimates the total change in homes (1.31 times observed). The
baseline matches the total by construction.
\item \textbf{Not predicted.} No method predicts job change at block level (engine $r = 0.068$).
\item \textbf{Not validated.} Access, mix, green cover and runoff have no observed after-change data, and are marked
as not validated in the Studio.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Likelihood of redevelopment}\label{sec:r-likely}

The redevelopment model ranks lots forward in time.
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Five years.} Trained on 2015--2020 outcomes and tested on 2020--2025, it reaches an AUC of
0.847, against 0.754 for the best simple baseline and 0.809 for a graph neural network.
\item \textbf{Top of the ranking.} Of the top 1\% of lots it ranks, 26\% were redeveloped, against a base
rate of 1.35\%.
\item \textbf{Calibration.} Its probabilities are well calibrated (expected calibration error 0.011).
\item \textbf{Rolling origins.} Across 15 origins from 2016 to 2025, with horizons of one, three and five years,
its out-of-time AUC is 0.847--0.952, above the best simple baseline at every origin.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{What zoning and plans add, across seven cities}\label{sec:r-layers}

Existing conditions alone rank the lots that developed with an out-of-time AUC of 0.824--0.911 in
six cities, and 0.571 in San Diego, where the one-year window recorded few changes (Appendix
Table~\ref{tab:auc}).
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Context} adds the most (Table~\ref{tab:gains}, Figure~\ref{fig:gains}): from +0.020 to
+0.116, significantly in five cities. Phoenix is the exception: its regional land-use series
starts in 2022, so recent change is unknown in its training window.
\item \textbf{Zoning} carries information of its own. Without context, it raises AUC significantly in five of seven
cities. Developed lots were 2.1 to 9.5 times as likely as other lots to have a zoning
class outside their existing use group.
\item \textbf{Overlap.} Most of that information is shared with existing conditions and context: developed lots were
also 3.5 to 19 times as likely to be vacant. Over context, zoning adds a significant gain
in four of seven cities and the plan in three of four, at most +0.021 outside Phoenix. There, zoning adds
+0.049 and the plan +0.054, and 45\% of developed lots were vacant.
\item \textbf{Conservative variant.} The plan gain in San Diego and the zoning gain in Chicago do not survive the conservative variant, so those gains came from
lots rezoned or re-planned during the study.
\end{itemize}

The layers matter more for what a developing lot becomes (Table~\ref{tab:dest}). In all six cities with a
destination, the zoning class names the new class correctly more often than the existing use, by 12 to
64 percentage points. In Phoenix and San Diego development is a change of class by definition, so there
the existing use is never right at class level. In Dallas the plan class is right for 80\% of developed
lots, against 61\% for zoning. A model fitted on other cities predicts less well than the city's own
model in four of five cities (Appendix Table~\ref{tab:transfer}).

\subsection{Scenario projections}\label{sec:r-homes}

Capacity projections overstate near-term housing by two orders of magnitude (Table~\ref{tab:homes}).
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Build-out.} In four cities, zoning and plan build-out exceed the homes added in the test window
76- to 193-fold. Part of the gap is definitional, since build-out is an end state rather than a two-year
flow.
\item \textbf{Likelihood weighting} brings the totals to 0.81--2.64 times the observed.
\item \textbf{Trend.} A five-year trend ranks districts better: Spearman 0.51 to 0.81, against
$-$0.37 to 0.55 for the likelihood-weighted projections, better in all four cities.
\end{itemize}

The Manhattan rezonings show the same contrast for single decisions (Table~\ref{tab:replay},
Figure~\ref{fig:replay}). Capacity projected 8{,}423 homes on development sites, or 5{,}207 pro-rated to
2025. The likelihood-weighted projection gave 585, against 561 built, and the observed count lies
within its 95\% range in two of three rezonings.

\subsection{Optimizer and plausibility}\label{sec:r-opt}

\paragraph{Optimality.} On 20 small study areas where every plan with up to two changes can be enumerated,
first-order search alone found the exact optimum in 73\% of areas, and with exact re-scoring in
93\% (median 0.28 s). At district scale (Table~\ref{tab:opt}), exact greedy search found the best
plan in all 12 districts but took a median 25.87 s. First-order search with exact
re-scoring reached a median 97.4\% of that score in 1.14 s, the speed used in the Studio.

\paragraph{Plausibility.} Recommended plans test plausibility against what happened next (Table~\ref{tab:realism}).
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Without realism layers}, 17\% of recommended changes had no precedent in the city.
\item \textbf{With the likelihood layer}, 21\% of recommended parcels were redeveloped by 2025, against
12\% without it, 1.4\% of all lots and 5.2\% of the likeliest fifth.
\item \textbf{The cost} is a lower plan score: 2.73 against 8.27. What is plausible and what
the objective prefers differ, and the Studio shows both.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Decision rules}\label{sec:r-dec}

In the simulated stakeholder scenario for 12 Manhattan districts, the decision rule changes the outcome.
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Agreement.} Across the 12 districts, the nine rules never all agree; a Condorcet winner exists in
seven.
\item \textbf{Other choices.} The residents' referendum picks the council's plan in one district, and the
council's winner is never the Nash bargaining solution.
\item \textbf{Manipulability.} One insincere ballot could change the Schulze result in six
districts.
\item \textbf{Robustness.} The winner survives a median 76\% of joint perturbations of coefficients and
seats, and 54\% of redrawn stakeholder weights.
\end{itemize}
These numbers describe the simulated scenario, not public opinion. They show that a recommendation should be
reported with the rule that produced it, and with how it changes under others.

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{What a planner gets.} For any proposed change, PlanArena shows its effects across 11
indicators with ranges, and whether zoning and the plan allow it. It also shows how likely the change is, what the
optimizer would recommend instead, and how the choice depends on the decision rule. Each of these outputs has a
stated test against observed data (Table~\ref{tab:design}), and indicators without one are labelled. This answers, for
one system, the gap between the claimed and demonstrated contributions of planning support systems and urban twins
\citep{vonk2005,azadi2025,kruse2026}.

\paragraph{Design guidance.} The results support four practices for decision support tools.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Use each layer for the question it answers.} Zoning and the adopted plan add little to predicting
\emph{where} development happens once existing conditions and context are known, but they help predict \emph{what}
it becomes, and they bound \emph{how much} a site can hold. This is consistent with evidence that rezoning follows
opportunity \citep{gabbe2018}, that upzoning's short-run effect on construction varies \citep{freemark2020,dong2024,
greenaway2023}, and that plans are partly implemented \citep{laurian2004,berke2006}.
\item \textbf{Report likelihood-weighted projections beside capacity,} and a trend baseline beside both. Capacity
overstates near-term housing by orders of magnitude, and the trend ranked districts better than any projection.
\item \textbf{Constrain optimization by plausibility, and show the cost.} Realism layers change what is recommended
and lower the objective; both views belong in front of the planner.
\item \textbf{Report decisions with their rule.} No rule agreed with all the others in any district of the simulated scenario.
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{Limitations.}
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Impacts} are validated only in Manhattan. In the other nine cities the engine uses national or regional
coefficients, and its outputs there are unvalidated estimates.
\item \textbf{Indicators.} Job change at block level, access, mix, green cover and runoff after a change have no
observed test.
\item \textbf{Cross-city test.} The windows are short (one or two years), outcome definitions differ by city, and in
Dallas the plan and zoning are current layers without dates, so its gains are upper bounds.
\item \textbf{Optimizer and votes.} The optimizer is heuristic, and the votes rest on assumed utilities.
\item \textbf{Use.} Usability and use with planners are not evaluated here.
\item \textbf{Causation.} Nothing here estimates what zoning or plans cause.
\end{itemize}

\section{Conclusion}

PlanArena gives planners the effects of any parcel-level land-use change across social, economic and environmental
indicators, together with what is permitted, planned, likely and recommended. It runs on official data for ten large
US cities at interactive speed, and each component is tested against what happened. The tests also refine how such
systems should work:
\begin{itemize}
\item regulatory layers are best used for what development becomes and how much it could hold, not where it happens;
\item likelihood-weighted projections are far closer to what was built than capacity, while trends rank districts
better;
\item recommendations change when they must be plausible, and with the rule used to choose among them.
\end{itemize}
The code, data manifest and results are open, so the system and its tests can be extended to other cities.

\section*{Data and code availability}

The code, the result files behind every number, the figures and a manifest of every input (URL, retrieval date and
SHA-256) are in the PlanArena repository; \texttt{make reproduce} rebuilds the data and results from public sources.
Each city's ingestion report documents coverage, crosswalks and estimated fields. Owner and mailing fields in
assessor records were never requested or read. No human participants were involved.

\section{Digitising plans published as PDF maps}\label{app:digitise}

Philadelphia2035's land-use recommendations exist only as ``Proposed Land Use'' maps in 17 district plans
covering 18 districts. The maps are vector drawings in which each lot is a filled shape. They are
converted in six steps:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Legend.} The legend's swatch colours and labels are read.
\item \textbf{Colours.} Map colours are matched one to one to legend colours by perceptual distance (CIELAB $\Delta
E$, Hungarian assignment), refusing pairs further apart than $\Delta E = 45$.
\item \textbf{Visibility.} Only shapes that the rendered page actually shows are kept (maps are often clipped to the
district), and only the largest map frame on the page spread.
\item \textbf{Registration.} A similarity transform is fitted: the rendered footprint is first matched as an image
to the district's parcels and outline (FFT translation, Dice score), then refined by iterative closest point
\citep{reddy1996,besl1992,umeyama1991}.
\item \textbf{Classification.} Each parcel takes the category of the smallest shape containing its interior point.
\item \textbf{Checks.} A map is used only if the median parcel-to-shape distance is at most 10 ft and its plan agrees
with existing use clearly more often than the same map shifted 300 ft.
\end{enumerate}

Maps from 15 of 17 plans passed, covering 16 districts and
83\% of parcels.
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Registration.} Median errors were 1.1--7.2 ft (median 3.2 ft).
\item \textbf{Falsification test.} The digitised plans agree with the existing use on 60\%--90\%
of parcels, against 42\%--66\% for shifted maps.
\item \textbf{Failures.} The maps of South and West Park also draw neighbouring districts and failed registration.
\end{itemize}
Earlier map-processing work addresses scanned raster maps \citep{chiang2014,luft2021,milleville2022}; vector exports
allow the shapes to be read directly.
